description: The reasoning behind Site Reliability Engineering (SLIs/SLOs, error budgets and burn rates, alerting philosophy, incident response, blameless postmortems, capacity and release) and modern observability (Prometheus metrics model, structured events, distributed tracing, OpenTelemetry, Kubernetes platform signals). For a cloud/Kubernetes platform architect.

notes.front: What is Site Reliability Engineering, in Ben Treynor's one-line definition?
notes.back: "What happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team": running production with engineering, not with headcount.
notes.extra: Consequence: SREs are hired as engineers, write code, and are measured on reliability and on how little manual work the service needs.

notes.front: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) vs traditional ops: what is the structural difference?
notes.back: Ops scales people with load and handles failure by hand; SRE caps manual work, automates it away, and treats reliability as a software problem.
notes.analogy: Ops is bailing water faster as the boat grows; SRE is redesigning the hull so it leaks less.

notes.front: Why does the classic dev/ops split produce conflict rather than cooperation?
notes.back: Devs are rewarded for velocity, ops for stability. Opposed incentives make each side build walls: launch gates, change freezes, slow reviews.
notes.extra: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)'s fix: replace the political negotiation with a shared, objective number: the error budget.

notes.front: Embracing risk: why does Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) refuse to target 100% reliability?
notes.back: Past some point users can't tell (their phone, Wi-Fi and ISP fail more often), while each extra nine costs roughly 10× more. Spend that on features.
notes.analogy: A bridge rated for 100× its heaviest truck isn't safer in practice; it is just expensive.

notes.text: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) defines toil as work that is {{c1::manual}}, {{c2::repetitive}}, {{c3::automatable}}, {{c4::tactical / interrupt-driven}}, {{c5::without enduring value}} and {{c6::scaling linearly with service growth}}.
notes.extra: Test: if the service doubled in size, would this work double too? Then it's toil.

notes.front: Why does Google cap toil at 50% of an Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) team's time?
notes.back: To guarantee at least half the time goes into engineering that reduces future toil. Above 50% the team drifts into being a plain ops team.
notes.extra: Measured: teams track toil in surveys and on-call load; exceeding the cap is escalated, not absorbed.

notes.front: What does not count as toil, even though it isn't feature work?
notes.back: Overhead (meetings, reviews, HR paperwork) and real engineering such as designing automation. Toil is specifically the hands-on work of running the service.

notes.front: Beyond lost hours, why is toil harmful to an Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) organisation?
notes.back: It stalls careers, burns people out, sets the precedent that devs can offload operations, and slows the service's own progress.

notes.front: In the Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) view, when should a runbook step be turned into code?
notes.back: As soon as it is written down precisely enough for a human to follow mechanically: at that point it is specified well enough to automate.
notes.analogy: A recipe followed by rote is a program waiting for a computer.

notes.text: Google's release engineering rests on: a {{c1::self-service}} model (teams release without a release engineer), {{c2::high velocity}} (small frequent releases), {{c3::hermetic}} builds and {{c4::enforcement of policies}} via tooling.

notes.front: Why does Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) insist on hermetic builds?
notes.back: The build depends only on pinned tool and library versions, not on the machine's state, so any old release can be rebuilt to patch it.
notes.analogy: A hermetically sealed jar: what's inside is the same whoever opens it, wherever, whenever.

notes.front: Why does Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) want production software to be "boring"?
notes.back: Surprise is the enemy of reliability. Essential complexity is accepted; accidental complexity (clever abstractions, unused flags) is pushed back.
notes.extra: Pitfall: "it's stable because nobody changes it" is not boring, it's fragile. Stability must survive change.

notes.front: Why does Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) treat deleted code ("negative lines") as a reliability win?
notes.back: Every line is a liability: a place for bugs and a cost to understand. Dead code and unused flags still break, confuse and need maintenance.

notes.front: What is a Production Readiness Review (PRR), and what is it for?
notes.back: The gate before Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) takes on-call for a service: design, monitoring, capacity, dependencies and release process are reviewed and fixed first.
notes.extra: Also: the main way the "wisdom of production" flows back into design; the SRE Workbook recommends involving SRE far earlier than the PRR.

notes.front: What does it mean for Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) to "hand back the pager", and why is that threat useful?
notes.back: If a service exceeds its agreed ops load or ignores its error-budget policy, on-call duty returns to the developers. It keeps the incentives honest.

notes.front: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) vs DevOps: how do they relate?
notes.back: DevOps is a philosophy (break silos, automate, measure, accept failure). SRE is one concrete implementation with specific practices: Service Level Objectives (SLOs), error budgets, toil caps.
notes.extra: Google's phrasing: class SRE implements interface DevOps.

notes.front: What is a Service Level Indicator (SLI)?
notes.back: A quantitative measure of one aspect of the service as users experience it, usually a ratio: good events ÷ valid events.
notes.analogy: The speedometer reading, as opposed to the speed limit (SLO) and the fine (SLA).
notes.extra: Examples: fraction of requests served without 5xx; fraction of requests faster than 300 ms; fraction of data fresher than 10 min.

notes.front: What is a Service Level Objective (SLO)?
notes.back: A target for an Service Level Indicator (SLI) over a window, e.g. "99.9% of valid requests succeed in under 300 ms over 30 days".

notes.front: What is a Service Level Agreement (SLA)?
notes.back: A contract with customers that attaches consequences (credits, penalties) to missing stated service levels.
notes.extra: Rule of thumb: no consequence, no SLA; it's just an Service Level Objective (SLO) you published.

notes.front: Service Level Objective (SLO) vs Service Level Agreement (SLA): how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: An SLA has external consequences and is negotiated with customers; an SLO is the internal engineering target. The SLO is normally stricter.
notes.analogy: SLO is the speed you drive at; SLA is the limit the camera fines you for.

notes.front: Why set the internal Service Level Objective (SLO) tighter than the Service Level Agreement (SLA)?
notes.back: The gap is your reaction time: missing the SLO triggers engineering action before the contract (and money) is breached.

notes.front: Why express Service Level Indicators (SLIs) as a ratio of good to valid events rather than raw numbers or quantiles?
notes.back: A 0–100% scale works for every SLI, turns directly into an error budget, and lets you combine SLIs across journeys with the same machinery.

notes.front: In an Service Level Indicator (SLI), why distinguish valid events from all events?
notes.back: To exclude what you cannot be responsible for, e.g. malformed requests or client 4xx errors. Otherwise a buggy client burns your budget.
notes.analogy: A pizzeria's delivery time shouldn't count orders placed with a wrong address.
notes.extra: Pitfall: exclude too much and the SLI stops describing user experience; document the validity rule.

notes.front: How should you choose which Service Level Indicators (SLIs) to define?
notes.back: Start from user journeys ("browse", "checkout") and ask what the user would notice. Measure that, not CPU or queue depth.
notes.analogy: A restaurant's SLI is "meals served hot within 20 minutes", not "oven temperature".

notes.text: The Service Level Indicator (SLI) menu by service type: request-driven services use {{c1::availability}} and {{c2::latency}} (and quality); pipelines use {{c3::freshness}}, {{c4::correctness}} and coverage; storage uses {{c5::durability}}.

notes.front: Why define a latency Service Level Indicator (SLI) as "share of requests faster than X" rather than "99th percentile (p99) latency ≤ X"?
notes.back: The ratio form plugs into error budgets and burn rates; a quantile is not a ratio of good events and behaves badly at low traffic.
notes.extra: Equivalent: "99% of requests under 300 ms" is the same promise as "p99 ≤ 300 ms", but it's countable per request.

notes.front: Why can't you average percentiles across instances or time windows?
notes.back: A percentile is a property of the whole distribution; the mean of per-instance 99th percentiles (p99s) is not the fleet p99. Aggregate the histograms, then take the quantile.
notes.analogy: Averaging each classroom's tallest pupil doesn't give the school's tallest pupil.

notes.front: Request-based vs window-based Service Level Objective (SLO): what's the difference?
notes.back: Request-based: good requests ÷ all requests over the window. Window-based: share of short time windows (e.g. 1-minute) that met the criterion.
notes.analogy: Grading a shop by customers served happily (request-based) versus by minutes the door was open (window-based).

notes.front: What is the practical consequence of a request-based Service Level Objective (SLO) during traffic peaks?
notes.back: Errors at peak hit more requests and burn more budget; the same outage at 3 a.m. costs little. Budget tracks user harm, not clock time.
notes.extra: Window-based SLOs weigh every minute equally, which suits 'it must always be up' systems but ignores how many users were affected.

notes.text: Allowed downtime per year: 99% ≈ {{c1::3.65 days}}; 99.9% ≈ {{c2::8.8 hours}}; 99.99% ≈ {{c3::53 minutes}}; 99.999% ≈ {{c4::5.3 minutes}}.
notes.extra: Per 30 days: 99.9% ≈ 43 min, 99.99% ≈ 4.3 min. Each extra nine divides allowed downtime by 10.

notes.front: In what sense is an Service Level Objective (SLO) a budget for change?
notes.back: 100% − SLO is the unreliability you may spend. Risky releases, experiments and migrations are legitimate ways to spend it, as long as it lasts.
notes.analogy: A monthly allowance: spend it on something, don't hoard it, don't overdraw.

notes.front: Why is consistently exceeding your Service Level Objective (SLO) by a wide margin also a problem?
notes.back: Users come to depend on the unofficial level, and you have been too conservative with change. Either tighten the SLO or spend the budget.
notes.extra: Google's trick: Chubby injects planned outages so clients don't assume it never fails.

notes.front: How does a serial critical dependency bound your achievable Service Level Objective (SLO)?
notes.back: You can't be more available than a dependency you need for every request. A 99.9% dependency caps you below 99.9% unless you add redundancy or a fallback.
notes.analogy: A chain is no stronger than its weakest link; two links in series are weaker than either.

notes.front: Why measure an availability Service Level Indicator (SLI) at the load balancer rather than inside the application?
notes.back: The LB sees requests the app never received (crashes, overload, timeouts). App-side metrics make a dead backend look perfectly healthy.
notes.analogy: Ask the receptionist how many callers got through, not the staff who answered.
notes.extra: Closer still: client-side telemetry (real user monitoring (RUM)) also sees DNS, content delivery network (CDN) and network failures, at the cost of noise.

notes.front: Achievable vs aspirational Service Level Objective (SLO): where should a new SLO start?
notes.back: Start from what the service actually achieves today (achievable), publish that, then move stepwise toward the level users need (aspirational).

notes.front: Why must Service Level Objectives (SLOs) be reviewed periodically?
notes.back: User expectations, traffic and architecture change. An SLO that never alerts or never passes has stopped describing reality and should be re-set.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: What is an error budget?
notes.back: 1 − Service Level Objective (SLO): the amount of unreliability the service may accumulate over the SLO window before the objective is missed.
notes.analogy: A fixed monthly allowance of failure; every bad request is a coin spent.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: Service Level Objective (SLO) 99.9% over 30 days, 10 million valid requests. How big is the error budget?
notes.back: 0.1% of 10 M = 10,000 failed requests for the whole window.
notes.extra: In practice: a 20-minute full outage at 10 req/s burns 12,000, so one bad release can spend more than a month's budget.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: What is burn rate?
notes.back: How fast you are consuming error budget relative to the rate that would exhaust it exactly at the end of the window. Burn rate 1 = on track to use 100%.
notes.analogy: Fuel burn: at rate 1 the tank empties as you reach the destination; at rate 2 you're stranded halfway.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: How do you compute burn rate from an observed error ratio?
notes.back: \( \text{burn rate} = \dfrac{\text{observed error ratio}}{1-\text{SLO}} \). Service Level Objective (SLO) 99.9% and 1% errors → 0.01 / 0.001 = 10.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: At burn rate 14.4 on a 30-day window, how much budget disappears in one hour?
notes.back: 2%. One hour is 1/720 of the window; 14.4 × 1/720 = 0.02. Sustained, the whole budget is gone in about two days.
notes.extra: Formula: time to exhaustion = window ÷ burn rate = 720 h ÷ 14.4 ≈ 50 h.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: Why alert on burn rate rather than "error ratio above the Service Level Objective (SLO) threshold"?
notes.back: A threshold over a short window fires on noise; over a long window it fires too late. Burn rate expresses how urgently the budget is being lost.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: In multi-window burn-rate alerting, why combine a long window with a short one?
notes.back: The long window (e.g. 1 h) proves the burn is significant; the short window (e.g. 5 min) proves it is still happening, so the alert resets quickly once fixed.
notes.analogy: A fire alarm that needs both a hot room (1 h) and smoke right now (5 min) before it rings, and goes quiet once the smoke clears.
notes.extra: Rule of thumb: short window ≈ 1/12 of the long window.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: Why use multiple burn rates (fast and slow) rather than one?
notes.back: A fast burn (outage) must page within minutes; a slow leak (1× over days) would never trip a fast alert but still exhausts the budget. Slow burns become tickets.
notes.analogy: A burst pipe and a dripping tap both empty the tank; you need a different alarm for each.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.text: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) Workbook burn-rate tiers: 2% of budget in 1 h = burn rate {{c1::14.4}} (page); 5% in 6 h = burn rate {{c2::6}} (page); 10% in 3 days = burn rate {{c3::1}} (ticket).
notes.extra: Derivation: rate = budget fraction × (window ÷ alert window), e.g. 0.02 × 720 h / 1 h = 14.4.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: Why does burn-rate alerting break down for low-traffic services, and what helps?
notes.back: With few requests one error is a huge ratio, so alerts flap. Fixes: longer windows, synthetic traffic to raise the denominator, or a looser Service Level Objective (SLO).

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: What is an error budget policy?
notes.back: A document agreed by dev, Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) and product that says what happens when the budget is exhausted or nearly so, and who decides.
notes.extra: Typical clauses: feature freeze until budget recovers; reliability work prioritised; postmortem required; escalation path when teams disagree.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: Why must the error budget policy be agreed in advance and signed off by leadership?
notes.back: In the moment, shipping pressure wins every argument. A pre-commitment with executive backing makes the trade-off enforceable when it hurts.
notes.analogy: Ulysses tied to the mast: decide the rule before you hear the sirens.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: When the budget is exhausted and a release freeze applies, what may still ship?
notes.back: Changes that improve reliability, security fixes and rollbacks. Feature launches wait until the rolling window recovers budget.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: Error budget vs incident count: why is the budget the better reliability measure?
notes.back: The budget weighs each incident by user harm (bad events); a count treats a one-minute blip and a three-hour outage the same.
notes.analogy: Counting car accidents says nothing about whether they were fender-benders or write-offs.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: What does unspent budget near the end of a window tell you?
notes.back: You're taking too little risk. Use it: faster rollouts, chaos experiments, a risky migration. Budget doesn't carry over.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::03 Error Budgets & Burn Rate
notes.front: Rolling vs calendar Service Level Objective (SLO) window: what's the trade-off?
notes.back: Rolling (last 30 days) keeps recent incidents visible and recovers smoothly. Calendar (this month) aligns with business reporting but resets the budget abruptly.

notes.text: The four golden signals of monitoring: {{c1::latency}}, {{c2::traffic}}, {{c3::errors}} and {{c4::saturation}}.
notes.extra: Minimum viable monitoring: if you can measure only four things about a user-facing system, measure these.

notes.front: Why is saturation the forward-looking golden signal?
notes.back: It measures how full the constrained resource is (queue depth, memory, connections). It predicts failure before errors or latency show it.
notes.analogy: Water level in a dam: nothing is wrong yet, but you can see the overflow coming.

notes.front: Why track the latency of failed requests separately from successful ones?
notes.back: Fast failures (immediate 500s) pull the average down and hide slowness; slow failures are the worst case: the user waited and got nothing.

notes.front: Golden signals vs RED: what does RED leave out, and why?
notes.back: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) drops saturation. It's a request-centric view of a service; saturation belongs to resources, which utilisation, saturation, errors (USE) covers.

notes.front: In the utilisation, saturation, errors (USE) method, utilisation vs saturation?
notes.back: Utilisation: fraction of time the resource was busy. Saturation: extra work it couldn't serve, queued or waiting. A resource can be 100% utilised with zero saturation.
notes.analogy: A checkout till: utilisation is how often the cashier is busy; saturation is the length of the queue.

notes.front: Symptom-based vs cause-based alerting: which should page, and why?
notes.back: Page on symptoms users feel (Service Level Indicator (SLI) dropping). Causes are many and change over time; one cause can trigger a flood, and a cause with no symptom isn't urgent.
notes.extra: Example: "disk 90% full" is a cause → ticket. "Error ratio burning budget at 14×" is a symptom → page.

notes.text: A page must be {{c1::urgent}} (needs a human now), {{c2::actionable}} (there's something to do), {{c3::novel}} (not a repeat of another alert) and {{c4::require intelligence}} (otherwise automate it).

notes.front: Page vs ticket vs log: how do you decide the delivery channel for an alert?
notes.back: Page: must be acted on now. Ticket: must be fixed within days. Log/dashboard: useful for diagnosis only. Anything paged that could wait is fatigue.

notes.front: What is alert fatigue, and what does it cost?
notes.back: Repeated non-actionable alerts teach responders to ignore alerts. Real incidents get missed, and on-callers burn out.
notes.analogy: Car alarms: everyone has learned they mean nothing, so nobody looks.

notes.front: Black-box vs white-box monitoring: what does each tell you?
notes.back: Black-box probes the service from outside, like a user: "it is broken now". White-box reads internals (metrics, logs): "it is about to break, and here's why".
notes.analogy: Black-box is the mystery shopper; white-box is the kitchen's own thermometers.

notes.front: Why keep black-box probes even with rich white-box metrics?
notes.back: Internal metrics can't see failures outside the process: DNS, certificates, load balancers, a region that vanished. Probes validate the whole path end to end.

notes.text: Evaluating an alerting rule: {{c1::precision}} (share of alerts that were real), {{c2::recall}} (share of real incidents alerted), {{c3::detection time}} and {{c4::reset time}} (how long it keeps firing after the fix).

notes.front: What three questions should you ask of every existing alert when pruning?
notes.back: Did anyone act on it? Was it urgent, or could it have waited? Would another alert have caught the same problem? Three "no"s → delete it.

notes.front: Dashboards vs alerts: what is each for?
notes.back: Alerts interrupt a human for a decision. Dashboards answer "what is going on?" during investigation. Never add an alert to replace looking at a graph.
notes.analogy: The pager is a fire alarm; the dashboard is the building's floor plan you consult after it rings.

notes.front: Monitoring vs observability: how does the Honeycomb school distinguish them?
notes.back: Monitoring watches known failure modes with predefined checks. Observability lets you ask new questions of the system from outside without shipping new code.
notes.analogy: Monitoring is a dashboard of warning lights; observability is being able to pop the hood and probe anything.
notes.extra: Key phrase: unknown unknowns. You cannot pre-aggregate your way to a question you haven't thought of yet.

notes.front: Why should every page link to a playbook?
notes.back: It cuts time to mitigation, reduces variance between responders, and shows which alerts are mechanical enough to automate away.

notes.front: How does PromQL rate() handle a counter reset (process restart)?
notes.back: A drop in value is read as a reset to zero and the increase continues from there, so restarts don't produce negative rates.
notes.extra: Pitfall: a reset within the window loses the counts accumulated just before it; keep windows short relative to restart frequency.

notes.front: Why must a rate() range be at least 2× (ideally 4×) the scrape interval?
notes.back: rate() needs at least two samples in the range; with fewer it returns nothing. 4× tolerates a missed scrape without gaps in the graph.

notes.front: Why does increase(http_requests_total[5m]) return fractional values like 2.5?
notes.back: It is rate() × window seconds, extrapolated to the window edges from the samples inside it. It estimates, it doesn't count.
notes.analogy: Estimating how far a car drove from two odometer glances and assuming constant speed in between.

notes.front: Why should "items processed" be a counter, not a gauge of "items per minute"?
notes.back: A counter survives missed scrapes and can be rated over any window; a per-minute gauge bakes one window into the exporter and loses data when a scrape is skipped.

notes.front: Why is a gauge of "last request latency" almost useless?
notes.back: Scraped every 15 s, it shows one arbitrary request out of thousands. Latency is a distribution: use a histogram.

notes.front: Why are Prometheus histogram buckets cumulative (le = "less than or equal")?
notes.back: So buckets can be summed across instances and dropped without breaking others, and a single bucket already answers "how many requests under X?".
notes.analogy: Nested measuring cups: the 1-litre cup already contains everything the 300 ml cup would.

notes.front: Why put a histogram bucket boundary exactly at your Service Level Objective (SLO) latency threshold?
notes.back: histogram_quantile interpolates linearly inside a bucket, so it's only exact at an edge. With an edge at 300 ms, bucket{le="0.3"} / count is your exact Service Level Indicator (SLI).

notes.front: Native (exponential) histograms vs classic buckets: what changes?
notes.back: Bucket edges follow a fixed growth factor, so no manual choice; buckets are sparse, one series instead of N, and higher resolution at lower cost.
notes.extra: Also: histograms of different resolutions still merge. OpenTelemetry's exponential histogram is the same idea.

notes.front: What does one time series cost in Prometheus, and what drives memory?
notes.back: Each unique label combination is a series kept in memory (head block) with its index. Memory scales with active series, not with sample volume.

notes.front: Why does label churn hurt Prometheus more than a stable high series count?
notes.back: Every new label value creates a new series; pod names, request IDs or build hashes keep creating them, so the index grows without bound and queries slow.
notes.analogy: A library can hold many books, but a new shelf for every borrower each day wrecks the catalogue.

notes.front: A metric has labels with 10, 50 and 100 possible values. How many series can it create per target?
notes.back: Up to 10 × 50 × 100 = 50,000. Cardinality multiplies across labels; across 200 targets that's 10 million series.

notes.front: How are recording rules used specifically for Service Level Objectives (SLOs)?
notes.back: Precompute the Service Level Indicator (SLI) error ratio at several windows (5m, 1h, 6h, 3d) as named series, so burn-rate alerts and dashboards are cheap and use one definition.
notes.extra: Naming convention: level:metric:operations, e.g. job:slo_errors_per_request:ratio_rate1h.

notes.front: What is staleness in Prometheus, and why does it matter for alerting?
notes.back: A series with no sample for 5 min (or whose target vanished) returns no value. A disappeared service produces nothing, not zero, so threshold alerts go silent.
notes.analogy: A silent smoke detector is not the same as a detector reporting no smoke.
notes.extra: Fix: alert on absent() or on up == 0 as well as on the Service Level Indicator (SLI).

notes.front: Federation vs remote write: when is each the right tool?
notes.back: Federation: a parent Prometheus scrapes a selected, aggregated subset from children (hierarchical). Remote write: stream everything to a central store for a global view and high availability (HA).
notes.analogy: Federation is a manager reading summary reports from branch offices; remote write is every branch mailing every receipt to head office.

notes.front: How does a highly available Prometheus pair work, and where are duplicates removed?
notes.back: Two identical servers scrape the same targets. Each adds an external replica label; the query layer (e.g. Thanos Query) deduplicates at read time.

notes.text: Prometheus naming: counters end in {{c1::_total}}; values use {{c2::base units}} (seconds, bytes, not ms or MB); the {{c3::unit}} is a suffix like _seconds.
notes.extra: Why: base units let any series be combined without conversion; the suffix makes rate(…_total) read as 'events per second'.

notes.front: Why log structured key–value / JSON records instead of printf-style sentences?
notes.back: Fields become queryable dimensions with no regex parsing; the same record can be filtered, grouped and counted by any key.
notes.extra: Example: {"event":"order_failed","user_id":42,"region":"eu-west","ms":812} instead of "Order for user 42 failed after 812ms".

notes.front: What is a wide event (canonical log line)?
notes.back: One record per request per service, emitted at the end, carrying all context: user, region, version, feature flags, timings, outcome.
notes.analogy: A flight data recorder entry per request, instead of 40 scattered cockpit remarks.
notes.extra: Origin: Stripe's canonical log lines; Honeycomb's events. One row answers questions you didn't anticipate, without joins.

notes.front: High cardinality vs high dimensionality: what's the difference?
notes.back: Cardinality: how many distinct values a field has (user_id: millions). Dimensionality: how many fields each event carries (hundreds). Observability wants both.

notes.front: Why do metrics choke on high cardinality while event stores don't?
notes.back: Metrics pre-aggregate at write time, one series per label combination. Event stores keep raw rows (often columnar) and aggregate at query time, so values cost nothing extra.

notes.front: What is the semantic line between ERROR and WARN log levels?
notes.back: ERROR: an operation failed and someone should look. WARN: something unexpected happened but was handled. If no one will ever act on it, it isn't an ERROR.

notes.front: What is a correlation ID, and how does it relate to the trace ID?
notes.back: A request-scoped ID copied into every log line the request produces, so logs can be stitched together. The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) trace ID is its standardised form.
notes.extra: In practice: put trace_id and span_id into every log record; then logs, traces and exemplars share one key.

notes.front: How should you sample logs without losing the signal?
notes.back: Keep 100% of errors and rare events, sample the flood of identical successes, and record the sample rate on each kept event so counts can be re-weighted.
notes.analogy: Keep every complaint letter, but only every hundredth thank-you note, and remember you kept one in a hundred.

notes.front: Where does the cost of logs come from, and why does it grow faster than you expect?
notes.back: Ingest, indexing and retention are billed per byte, and bytes scale with request volume × lines per request. Chatty INFO logs grow linearly with traffic.
notes.extra: Levers: drop DEBUG/INFO in prod, one wide event per request, tiered storage (hot 7 days, cold archive), sampling.

notes.front: When do logs beat metrics?
notes.back: When you need the specific case: which user, which request, the exact payload, a rare event, or a question you didn't define a metric for.

notes.front: When do metrics beat logs?
notes.back: For trends, alerting and long retention: millions of events collapse into a few cheap numbers that are fast to query and compare over months.

notes.front: What is the critique of the "three pillars" (metrics, logs, traces)?
notes.back: They are storage formats, not capabilities. Observability is the ability to answer new questions; a single stream of rich events can derive all three.

notes.front: How does a wide event relate to a span?
notes.back: A span is a wide event with timing and a parent pointer. Attach enough attributes to spans and they double as your structured logs.

notes.front: Why should containerised apps log to stdout and let an agent ship logs?
notes.back: The app stays ignorant of the logging backend; the platform collects, enriches (pod, namespace) and routes uniformly. Rotation and buffering stop being the app's problem.

notes.front: Why is personally identifiable information (PII) in logs an observability design problem, not only a legal one?
notes.back: Once stored, it is replicated to indexes, backups and vendors. Redact at the source or in the collector; never log raw request bodies or headers by default.

notes.front: When is deriving metrics from logs (counting ERROR lines) acceptable, and what is the pitfall?
notes.back: Fine as a stopgap or for third-party software you can't instrument. Pitfall: expensive, laggy and brittle: a reworded message silently breaks the alert.

notes.text: A span records an operation with a name, start and end time, a {{c1::span context}} (trace_id + span_id), a {{c2::parent span id}}, key–value {{c3::attributes}}, timestamped {{c4::events}} and a {{c5::status}}.

notes.front: What does a trace show that aggregate metrics never can?
notes.back: Where the time went in one specific request across services: the causal chain, the parallelism and the gaps between hops.
notes.analogy: Metrics are the airport's average delay; a trace is one passenger's itinerary showing exactly where the wait happened.

notes.text: World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) traceparent header: {{c1::00}}-{{c2::<32 hex trace-id>}}-{{c3::<16 hex parent-id>}}-{{c4::01}}: version, trace id, parent span id, flags (01 = sampled).

notes.front: traceparent vs tracestate: what is each for?
notes.back: traceparent carries the standard trace/span IDs and sampled flag. tracestate carries vendor-specific key–value pairs that must be forwarded untouched.

notes.front: Why did the industry need World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) Trace Context instead of vendor headers (B3, uber-trace-id)?
notes.back: Every hop, including proxies, meshes and SaaS, must forward the same header or the trace breaks. One standard header set made cross-vendor traces possible.
notes.analogy: A parcel tracking number only works if every courier along the route reads and forwards the same label.

notes.front: When do you use a span link instead of a parent–child relationship?
notes.back: When causality isn't a simple call: a consumer processing a batch of messages from many producers, or a job triggered long after the request. Links join traces without forcing a tree.

notes.front: How is trace context propagated across an async boundary such as a queue?
notes.back: The producer injects traceparent into message headers; the consumer extracts it and starts a CONSUMER span, usually linked (or parented) to the producer span.

notes.front: Why does tail sampling require a stateful, trace-ID-aware collector tier?
notes.back: The decision needs the whole trace (was there an error? how slow?), so all spans of a trace must land on the same collector and wait in memory until it completes.
notes.extra: Mechanics: a load-balancing exporter routes by trace_id to a gateway pool; a decision wait of ~10–30 s bounds memory.

notes.front: Why is head sampling cheap but blind?
notes.back: The root decides at the start with no knowledge of the outcome, so errors and slow requests are kept at the same rate as boring successes.
notes.analogy: Deciding which flights to investigate before take-off: you keep 1% of them, crashes included only by luck.

notes.front: Why must downstream services respect the parent's sampling decision?
notes.back: Otherwise traces have holes: a kept root with missing children, or orphan spans with no root. OpenTelemetry (OTel)'s default ParentBased sampler exists for this.

notes.front: How does an exemplar shorten the investigation of a latency Service Level Objective (SLO) alert?
notes.back: The histogram bucket that burned the budget carries trace IDs from that exact time and bucket, so you jump from the alert to a representative slow trace in one click.

notes.front: How is a service map produced from traces?
notes.back: Each CLIENT→SERVER span pair with service.name on both sides is an edge; aggregating edges gives the dependency graph with call rates and error rates.

notes.front: Baggage vs span attributes: what's the difference?
notes.back: Attributes describe one span and are stored. Baggage (World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) baggage header) is propagated to every downstream hop but is not recorded unless copied onto spans.
notes.analogy: Attributes are notes written in one hotel's guest book; baggage is the suitcase the traveller carries to every hotel.
notes.extra: Pitfalls: baggage travels in every request header: keep it tiny, never put personally identifiable information (PII) or secrets in it.

notes.front: What is the critical path of a trace, and why does it matter?
notes.back: The chain of spans whose durations add up to the root's latency. Optimising a span off the critical path (a parallel branch) changes nothing for the user.
notes.analogy: In a project plan, shortening a task with slack doesn't move the deadline.

notes.front: Why instrument both the CLIENT and the SERVER side of a call?
notes.back: The gap between the client span and the server span is network, TLS, proxy and queueing time. With only server spans that time is invisible.

notes.front: Why should you not compute Service Level Indicators (SLIs) from sampled traces?
notes.back: Sampling, especially tail sampling, biases what is kept toward errors and slow requests. SLIs need every event: use metrics, or metrics derived from spans before sampling.

notes.front: HTTP semantic conventions: when does a 4xx response set span status to ERROR?
notes.back: On a CLIENT span, yes (the call failed for the caller). On a SERVER span, no: a 4xx is the client's fault, not the server's. 5xx is ERROR on both.
notes.extra: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) link: this mirrors the 'valid events' rule in Service Level Indicators (SLIs): don't count the client's mistakes against your service.

notes.text: OpenTelemetry signals: {{c1::traces}}, {{c2::metrics}}, {{c3::logs}} and (newest) {{c4::profiles}}. Baggage is propagated context, not a signal of its own.

notes.front: Why does OpenTelemetry bundle all signals in one project rather than separate standards?
notes.back: Correlation: a shared context gives trace IDs in logs, exemplars in metrics and the same Resource on everything, through one software development kit (SDK) and one Collector.

notes.front: Why should a shared library depend only on the OpenTelemetry (OTel) API, never on the software development kit (SDK)?
notes.back: The API is a no-op until an application installs an SDK, so the library adds no vendor, exporter or config choice. The app owner decides what happens to the telemetry.
notes.analogy: A library logs through an interface; the application plugs in the logger.

notes.text: In the tracing software development kit (SDK) a {{c1::TracerProvider}} owns the {{c2::Resource}} and {{c3::Sampler}}, and feeds spans through a {{c4::SpanProcessor}} (usually Batch) to an {{c5::Exporter}}.

notes.front: Why route telemetry through a Collector instead of exporting straight from the app?
notes.back: Decouples apps from backends; gives retry, buffering, enrichment, redaction and fan-out in one place; and keeps backend credentials out of every pod.

notes.front: In a Collector pipeline, why is memory_limiter first and batch last?
notes.back: The limiter must refuse data before the process out-of-memory kills (OOMs), so it guards the entrance. Batching compresses right before export so nothing downstream un-batches it.
notes.analogy: The bouncer stands at the door, not at the bar; and you pack the boxes right before loading the truck.

notes.front: What does the k8sattributes processor do, and why do it in the Collector rather than the app?
notes.back: Maps the sender's pod IP to pod, namespace, deployment and node labels and stamps them on telemetry. Apps don't know this reliably; the Collector asks the API server once.

notes.front: Collector as sidecar vs node-level DaemonSet agent: what's the trade-off?
notes.back: Sidecar: per-pod isolation and config, but N copies of memory and a restart per app change. DaemonSet: one per node, shared and cheap, but a noisy pod can starve its neighbours.

notes.front: OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) over gRPC (4317) vs OTLP over HTTP/protobuf (4318): when choose which?
notes.back: gRPC: efficient streaming between services and collectors. HTTP: browsers, serverless, strict proxies and firewalls that can't speak HTTP/2 gRPC.

notes.front: Why is service.name the single most important resource attribute?
notes.back: It's the join key for everything: service maps, rate, errors, duration (RED) dashboards, log-to-trace links and Service Level Objectives (SLOs) all group by it. A missing or inconsistent name fragments the service.

notes.front: Resource attributes vs span attributes: how to decide where a value goes?
notes.back: Resource: facts about the producer that hold for all its telemetry (service, version, pod, cloud region). Span attribute: facts about this one operation (route, status, user tier).

notes.front: What does auto-instrumentation not give you?
notes.back: Business context. It knows frameworks (HTTP, DB, queues) but not your domain: order value, tenant, feature flag. Those need manual attributes or custom spans.

notes.front: Cumulative vs delta temporality in OpenTelemetry (OTel) metrics: what's the difference and who wants which?
notes.back: Cumulative: value since process start (Prometheus style). Delta: change since the last export (StatsD/Datadog style). The Collector can convert delta to cumulative, but needs state.
notes.analogy: Cumulative is the odometer; delta is the trip meter you reset after every reading.

notes.text: OpenTelemetry (OTel) metric instruments: {{c1::Counter}} (monotonic), {{c2::UpDownCounter}} (can decrease), {{c3::Histogram}} (distribution), and {{c4::Gauge}} (last value, often via an asynchronous callback).

notes.front: What is an OpenTelemetry (OTel) metrics View, and why does a platform team care?
notes.back: An software development kit (SDK)-side rule that changes aggregation, bucket boundaries or drops attributes for an instrument, with no code change. It is the cardinality control knob at the source.
notes.analogy: A dimmer switch on an instrument: turn down the detail without rewiring the lamp.

notes.front: What is the spanmetrics connector, and why is it valuable for Service Level Objectives (SLOs)?
notes.back: A Collector component that acts as exporter of one pipeline and receiver of another, turning spans into rate, errors, duration (RED) metrics. Place it before sampling and you get exact Service Level Indicators (SLIs) from traces.

notes.front: Why does OpenTelemetry not define a new user-facing logging API, unlike traces and metrics?
notes.back: Every language already has entrenched loggers. OTel provides a bridge/appender for them that attaches trace context and ships records as OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP), instead of asking the world to rewrite log calls.

notes.front: How can the Collector replace a Prometheus server for scraping?
notes.back: Its prometheus receiver reads scrape configs and service discovery; a prometheusremotewrite exporter sends to Mimir/Thanos. The Operator's Target Allocator shards targets across replicas.

notes.front: What happens in the Collector when the backend is down?
notes.back: The exporter's sending queue buffers and retries with backoff; when the queue is full, new data is dropped. A persistent (file-backed) queue survives a Collector restart.
notes.extra: Monitor it: otelcol_exporter_send_failed_* and queue size are the Collector's own Service Level Indicators (SLIs).

notes.front: Where does the Incident Command System come from, and why did Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) borrow it?
notes.back: From US firefighting (Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) ICS). It gives clear roles, a single decision-maker and a span of control that scales from one responder to dozens.

notes.text: Incident roles: the {{c1::Incident Commander}} owns decisions and delegates; the {{c2::Operations Lead}} does the hands-on work; the {{c3::Communications Lead}} updates stakeholders; the {{c4::Planning / Scribe}} role keeps the log and handles follow-ups.

notes.front: Why should the Incident Commander not debug?
notes.back: Heads-down debugging destroys situational awareness. The IC's job is to hold the whole picture, set priorities and decide, which no one else is doing.
notes.analogy: The conductor doesn't play an instrument during the concert.

notes.front: What is the live incident document for?
notes.back: A single shared source of truth: timeline, current theory, who is doing what, next update time. It enables handoffs and becomes the postmortem's raw material.

notes.front: What should define an incident's severity level?
notes.back: User impact and urgency (scope, Service Level Objective (SLO) budget being burned, data at risk), never the suspected cause. Severity sets response size and communication cadence.

notes.front: Why have a low threshold for declaring an incident?
notes.back: Standing down an unneeded response is cheap; ramping up late is expensive. Declaring early also starts the record and the communication clock.
notes.analogy: Calling the fire brigade for smoke and sending them home is cheaper than calling them for flames.

notes.front: What makes a handoff of the IC role safe?
notes.back: It is explicit and acknowledged: "You are now Incident Commander." "I have the incident." The gap where nobody is in command is the danger.

notes.text: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) Book on-call sizing: an engineer spends at most {{c1::25%}} of time on call, handles at most {{c2::two}} incidents per 12-hour shift, in a team of at least {{c3::8}} (single site) or 6 + 6 (multi-site).
notes.extra: Reasoning: primary + secondary rotations with 25% caps need 8 people; below that, either toil or burnout rises.

notes.front: When should an on-caller escalate, and why is it not a failure?
notes.back: When a time-box passes without progress, or the fix needs access or knowledge they lack. The goal is mitigation speed, not solving it alone.

notes.front: Why send status updates on a fixed cadence even when there's no news?
notes.back: "No change, next update at :30" stops stakeholders interrupting responders and builds trust that silence doesn't mean abandonment.

notes.front: MTTD vs MTTR: what does each measure?
notes.back: MTTD: mean time to detect, from fault to alert. MTTR: mean time to recover (or repair), from fault to users being fine again. Monitoring shrinks MTTD; mitigations shrink MTTR.

notes.front: Why is mean time between failures (MTBF) a weak target for distributed services, and why is even mean time to recover (MTTR) a shaky statistic?
notes.back: Frequent small failures with fast recovery beat rare huge ones, so chasing MTBF misleads. And incident durations are heavy-tailed, so a mean of a few dozen is mostly noise.
notes.extra: Reference: the VOID report (Courtney Nash) argues MTTR is too noisy to show improvement; track budget burn and learning instead.

notes.front: Why mitigate before you understand the cause?
notes.back: Users are hurting now; the root cause can wait. Rollback, failover, flag off or shed load first, then investigate on a stable system.
notes.analogy: Stop the bleeding before you work out why the patient fell.

notes.text: Generic mitigations to prepare in advance: {{c1::rollback}} the last change, {{c2::drain traffic}} to another region or cluster, {{c3::turn off a feature flag}}, {{c4::add capacity}} or shed low-priority load.
notes.extra: Why generic: they work before you know the cause; the Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) Workbook calls them the first thing to try.

notes.front: What makes a good runbook?
notes.back: Tied to one alert, says how to confirm the problem, how to mitigate, and links the dashboards; kept current by the on-call rotation. Pure steps with no judgement should be automated.

notes.front: What is chaos engineering?
notes.back: Experimenting on a system to build confidence in its behaviour under turbulence: state a steady-state hypothesis, inject a realistic fault, limit blast radius, compare.

notes.front: Why run chaos experiments in production?
notes.back: Only production has the real traffic, data, config and dependencies. A staging success proves little; a controlled production failure proves the hypothesis.

notes.front: Chaos engineering vs game day (Disaster Recovery Testing (DiRT)): what does each test?
notes.back: Chaos tests the system's tolerance to faults. A game day tests the people and process: paging, access, runbooks, communication, decision-making.
notes.extra: Typical game-day findings: expired credentials, stale runbooks, nobody knew who could approve a failover.

notes.front: What is the Wheel of Misfortune?
notes.back: Role-play training where an on-caller works through a past incident replayed by a game master. It builds judgement before the real page arrives.

notes.front: What makes a postmortem blameless?
notes.back: It assumes everyone acted in good faith with the information they had, and asks what in the system made that action reasonable and its outcome bad.

notes.front: Why is blame bad for reliability, not just for morale?
notes.back: Blamed people hide information, so the next postmortem learns less. People and incentives are part of the system; punishing them fixes nothing structural.

notes.front: Blameless vs no accountability: how do they differ?
notes.back: Accountability shifts from "who caused it" to "who owns fixing the conditions". Action items have owners and deadlines; people aren't punished for honest mistakes.

notes.text: Typical postmortem triggers: user-visible downtime beyond a threshold, {{c1::data loss}}, {{c2::on-call intervention}} (rollback, rerouting), resolution time over a threshold, and a {{c3::monitoring failure}} (found by a human, not an alert).

notes.front: Why prefer contributing factors over a single root cause?
notes.back: Complex systems fail when several normally harmless conditions combine. "Root cause" is just where you stopped looking; naming one hides the others.
notes.analogy: A plane crash report lists a dozen holes that lined up, not one.

notes.front: What is the limitation of Five Whys?
notes.back: Each "why" has several true answers, so following one chain produces a tidy story that reflects the asker's bias. Use it to branch, not to find 'the' cause.

notes.text: Good postmortem action items are classified as {{c1::prevent}} (stop recurrence), {{c2::detect}} (alert sooner) or {{c3::mitigate}} (recover faster), and tracked like bugs with owners and dates.

notes.front: Why do many postmortems fail to change anything?
notes.back: Action items untracked or too many, no review of the document, blame creeping in, and no sharing beyond the team. Writing it is 20% of the value.
notes.extra: Practice: postmortem review groups, a tracked backlog, and 'postmortem of the month' for visibility.

notes.front: What is hindsight bias, and how does it poison postmortems?
notes.back: Knowing the outcome makes it seem obvious in advance. "They should have seen it" judges people by information they did not have at the time.
notes.analogy: A detective novel is obvious on the second reading.

notes.front: Why avoid counterfactuals ("if only they had checked…") in a postmortem?
notes.back: They describe a world that didn't happen and explain nothing about why the real action made sense at the time. Ask what made the check seem unnecessary.

notes.front: What is normalisation of deviance?
notes.back: Small rule-bendings that don't fail become routine and the baseline shifts, until the accumulated deviation meets a condition it can't survive.
notes.analogy: Challenger: O-ring erosion was seen on earlier flights, didn't cause disaster, and became 'acceptable'.

notes.front: Safety-I vs Safety-II: how do they define safety?
notes.back: Safety-I: as few things as possible go wrong; study failures. Safety-II: as many things as possible go right under varying conditions; study everyday work too.

notes.front: Work-as-imagined vs work-as-done: why does the gap matter in incident analysis?
notes.back: Procedures describe imagined work; people adapt them daily to make the system work. Incidents expose the gap, and fixing the procedure alone widens it.

notes.front: Robustness vs resilience in the resilience-engineering sense?
notes.back: Robustness: withstanding anticipated faults by design (redundancy, limits). Resilience: adapting to the unanticipated, which mostly means people with slack, skill and authority.

notes.front: Dekker's old view vs new view of human error?
notes.back: Old view: human error causes failure, so remove or retrain the human. New view: human error is a symptom of deeper system trouble and the starting point of investigation.

notes.front: Why review near misses, not only incidents?
notes.back: Same mechanisms, no damage, far more frequent, and nobody is defensive, so you learn the same lessons cheaper and earlier.
notes.analogy: Aviation improved by studying the thousand near-collisions, not only the rare crash.

notes.front: What happens when incident count becomes a team key performance indicator (KPI)?
notes.back: Goodhart's law: incidents stop being declared, severities get downgraded, and learning stops. Incident data is for learning, not for performance reviews.

notes.text: The reflective part of a postmortem has three headings: what went {{c1::well}}, what went {{c2::wrong}}, and where we got {{c3::lucky}}.
notes.extra: Why 'lucky': it captures latent failures that didn't bite this time, the Safety-II angle inside the standard template.

notes.front: What are the three inputs of capacity planning in the Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) sense?
notes.back: A demand forecast (organic and inorganic growth), the lead time to provision, and headroom for failure and load tests. Then validate with regular load testing.

notes.front: Why provision N+2 rather than N+1?
notes.back: One unit may be down for planned maintenance or upgrade while another fails unexpectedly. N+1 leaves you at exactly N during every rollout.

notes.front: Organic vs inorganic growth in demand forecasting?
notes.back: Organic: steady adoption and usage trends you can extrapolate. Inorganic: step changes from launches, marketing, migrations or a new big customer; these must be collected from people.

notes.front: Why load-test to failure, not just to the planned peak?
notes.back: You need to know where the knee is and how the system fails (slow, erroring, cascading) before production finds out. Headroom is meaningless without the ceiling.
notes.analogy: You don't know a bridge's safety margin until you know the load that cracks it.

notes.text: Google's request criticality levels, shed from the bottom up: {{c1::CRITICAL_PLUS}} (user-visible, must not fail), {{c2::CRITICAL}}, {{c3::SHEDDABLE_PLUS}} (retries tolerated), {{c4::SHEDDABLE}} (batch, drop freely).
notes.extra: Point: load shedding is a policy question, criticality is propagated with the request so every layer sheds the same things first.

notes.front: Load shedding vs graceful degradation: how do they differ?
notes.back: Shedding refuses some requests cheaply to protect the rest. Degradation serves everyone a cheaper answer: cached, partial, fewer results, recommendations off.
notes.analogy: A full restaurant either turns people away at the door or serves a shorter menu to all.

notes.front: Why should retries happen at one layer only?
notes.back: Stacked retries multiply: three layers each retrying three times is 27× load on the bottom service during an outage. Retry at the edge, fail fast below.
notes.extra: Companions: retry budgets, backoff with jitter and circuit breakers are covered in the Distributed Systems deck.

notes.front: What is deadline propagation, and what does it prevent?
notes.back: Each hop passes the remaining time budget downstream and gives up when it is spent. Prevents servers working on requests the user has already abandoned.

notes.front: Why can adding capacity during a cascading failure fail to help?
notes.back: New instances start cold (empty caches, just-in-time (JIT), connections) and are swamped immediately by the queued load. Cut load first, then add capacity.

notes.front: What is a server's lame-duck state, and why have it?
notes.back: On shutdown it keeps serving but tells load balancers to stop sending new requests, then drains in-flight work. Avoids the errors of a hard stop during every deploy.
notes.analogy: A shop that locks the door to new customers but lets those inside finish paying.

notes.front: What is the statistical trap in judging a canary?
notes.back: A small canary sees little traffic, so its error rate is noisy. Compare it to a baseline of the same size and age, not to the whole fleet, and give it enough events.

notes.front: A service has a 99.9% Service Level Objective (SLO). Roughly how many requests must a canary see before a budget-level error rate is even observable?
notes.back: On the order of thousands: at 0.1% errors you expect one error per 1,000 requests, so a few hundred requests tell you nothing either way.

notes.front: Why roll out in exponentially growing stages (1% → 10% → 50% → 100%) with bake time?
notes.back: Early stages bound the blast radius while the error rate is unknown; later stages confirm at scale. Bake time lets slow failures (leaks, caches) show up.
notes.extra: Progressive-delivery mechanics (Argo Rollouts, Flagger) live in the Platform Engineering deck.

notes.front: From the Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) angle, what do feature flags buy you, and what do they cost?
notes.back: They decouple deploy from release and make 'flag off' the fastest mitigation. Costs: flag debt, untested flag combinations, and configuration becoming a change that needs the same care as code.

notes.front: Why does Google run Launch Coordination Engineering (launch reviews) as a dedicated function?
notes.back: A launch touches capacity, dependencies, rollback, monitoring and policy. A small team that has seen hundreds of launches catches what a first-time team cannot.

notes.front: Why must every release be rollback-able, and what does that imply for schema changes?
notes.back: Rollback is the universal mitigation. Schema and data changes must stay compatible with the previous version (expand, migrate, contract later), or rollback is a lie.

notes.front: Why are change freezes a double-edged sword?
notes.back: Most outages follow changes, so a freeze lowers risk this week. But changes pile up and ship as one big risky batch afterwards. Small, frequent, reversible changes are safer.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: cAdvisor vs kube-state-metrics: which answers which question?
notes.back: cAdvisor (inside the kubelet): resource usage of containers (CPU seconds, memory bytes). kube-state-metrics: state of API objects (pods pending, deployment replicas unavailable).
notes.extra: node_exporter covers the host itself: disk, network, kernel. Three exporters, three layers.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: Latency Service Level Objective (SLO) breaches while CPU utilisation looks low: which Kubernetes metric do you check?
notes.back: container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total vs …_periods_total. CPU limits throttle bursty pods even at low average usage.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.text: Control-plane health signals: API server {{c1::request latency and error rate}}, etcd {{c2::WAL fsync duration}} (99th percentile (p99) well under 10 ms), scheduler {{c3::pending pods / scheduling latency}}, and controller {{c4::workqueue depth}}.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: Why is etcd fsync latency the key control-plane Service Level Indicator (SLI)?
notes.back: Every write serialises through etcd's disk. Slow fsync delays raft heartbeats, triggers leader elections, and surfaces as API server timeouts cluster-wide.
notes.analogy: The whole cluster queues behind a single notary's signature; if the notary is slow, everyone waits.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: Who is the user in a platform team's Service Level Objective (SLO), and what journeys do you measure?
notes.back: The developer. Journeys: a deploy reaches Running within X s, the API answers, logs appear within Y s, a new namespace is ready in Z min.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: Why is time-to-schedule a user-facing Service Level Indicator (SLI) for a platform, not an internal detail?
notes.back: Developers experience it as 'my deploy is stuck'. It aggregates node capacity, quotas, admission webhooks and image pulls into one number they feel.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: Which parts of observability should a platform team own, and which must stay with tenants?
notes.back: Platform: Collector, storage, default dashboards, software development kit (SDK) config, cardinality limits. Tenants: their Service Level Indicators (SLIs), Service Level Objectives (SLOs), alerts and runbooks, because only they know what 'good' means.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.text: Levers to cut observability cost without losing signal: {{c1::drop unused metrics}} (relabeling), {{c2::cap cardinality}} per tenant, {{c3::tier retention}} (hot vs cold), and {{c4::sample}} traces and logs.
notes.extra: Scale: observability commonly runs at 10–30% of infrastructure spend; cardinality and log volume dominate.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: Why do most scraped metrics turn out to be never queried, and what do you do about it?
notes.back: Exporters emit everything by default and nobody prunes. Audit which series dashboards and rules actually use, then drop the rest with relabeling or Views.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: Why enforce per-tenant series limits in a shared metrics backend?
notes.back: One team's label explosion (a user ID label, a per-pod histogram) can out of memory (OOM) the ingesters for everyone. Limits turn a platform outage into one tenant's rejected samples.
notes.analogy: Circuit breakers per apartment keep one tenant's faulty toaster from blacking out the building.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: What does the OpenTelemetry Operator do?
notes.back: Manages Collector instances via an OpenTelemetryCollector custom resource definition (CRD) and injects auto-instrumentation into annotated pods via an Instrumentation CRD and a mutating webhook.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: How does the Operator inject auto-instrumentation without changing the image?
notes.back: The mutating webhook adds an init container that copies the agent into a shared volume and sets env vars (e.g. JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, OTEL_*) on the app container.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: What is continuous profiling?
notes.back: Always-on, low-overhead (~1% CPU, often extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF)) sampling of stack traces across the fleet, stored as time series, so you can ask which code burned CPU or memory at 3 a.m. last Tuesday.
notes.analogy: A security camera over the CPU, always recording, so you can rewind to the moment it got busy.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: When does profiling beat tracing?
notes.back: When the time is spent inside one process: Garbage collection (GC), serialisation, a hot loop. A span says 'this call took 800 ms'; a profile says which lines.
notes.extra: Link: profiles tagged with trace/span IDs let you jump from a slow span to its flame graph.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: Why export Kubernetes Events instead of relying on kubectl get events?
notes.back: Events are kept for only about an hour. Exporting them (event exporter, OpenTelemetry (OTel) k8sobjects) lets you correlate OOMKills, evictions and failed pulls with Service Level Objective (SLO) dips later.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: How do you make sure the alerting pipeline itself is working?
notes.back: A 'watchdog' alert that always fires, routed to a dead-man's switch that pages if the heartbeat stops. Plus meta-monitoring: a separate, simpler Prometheus or external probe watching the monitoring stack.
notes.analogy: A smoke detector that chirps to prove its battery is alive.

notes.deck: SRE & Observability::12 Observability for Kubernetes & Platforms
notes.front: How do semantic conventions let a platform ship 'golden dashboards' per service automatically?
notes.back: If every service emits http.server.request.duration with the same attributes and service.name, one templated rate, errors, duration (RED) dashboard and one Service Level Objective (SLO) rule set work for all of them.
